items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I went to New York and I learned from other musicians I was working with, Duke Ellington, working with Count Basie, and big bands.

ctx.x: Right. You know here’s the saxophones.

This is the brass over here and the reeds over here. And then you learn how to score. You put all this stuff in the score, that’s a whole different thing. I went to the Conservatory before I moved to New York. I was like 18 years old and I went to the Conservatory and I learned keyboard harmony and solfeggio and all that you know. And I learned how to write European music you know. Stravinsky or let’s say Beethoven or Mozart. I learned how to put it together. So now as I said, well how can I learn Duke Ellington…

see? Jazz wasn’t even considered music in a lot of camps you know. It was like rap music today, you know it was like, oh wow, that’s a whole different world, you know, ether. So I say, “Well that’s my interest.” So I went to New York and I learned from other musicians I was working with, Duke Ellington, working with Count Basie, and big bands. Ray Charles. And they was writing. They was writing for different groups and whatnot. Because like if you go to New York, at that particular time, you could actually — if…

items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: "My head is grounded in that sound although I write all kinds of ways... Oliver, Duke Ellington and my head is like that."

ctx.x: I just have this picture of you the next morning after a gig with him meeting someone for coffee and saying, “Man you should have seen what I did last night.”

That’s right. That’s right. I would talk about it. “This guy’s crazy, this guy’s nuts.” But guess what? He turned me on — I played a gig with him at a place called the Baby Grand in Harlem and we had to play a dance, we had to play like Duke Ellington and Fletcher Henderson, we had to play swing and a little bebop. Because he’d play like, he could play like Art Tatum on piano you know. Fletcher — you know he could play stride. Kind of remind you of Monk in a way, Thelonious Monk in a way, where he could play the…

played, it was called the Baby Grand Ballroom on 125th Street in Harlem, and we were playing “Satin Doll” and “It Don’t Mean a Thing” and some of those older tunes. And he liked the way I played that, when he played changes now. So I got to play tunes and he really liked that. You know I made the gig, really made it happen for him. He was very pleased. So a lot of times he’d call me to play these traditional dances, for social dancing. The people, you know two step foxtrots and all that kind of stuff. Tangos and…
